conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Thompson. I'm Dr. Patel, one of the neurology team doctors. You're here today for your fifth maintenance dose of high-dose methotrexate, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that's right. I’ve been feeling okay since my last dose, just the usual floaters in my vision.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. The floaters tend to improve after treatment and then come back later, is that accurate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. They fade for a few weeks, then slowly return. Not painful, just annoying.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s consistent with what we’ve seen before. We’ll proceed with your methotrexate infusion today as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need any tests before the infusion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve already checked your labs. Your kidney function looks stable, which is important because methotrexate can affect the kidneys. We’ll also give you IV fluids and sodium bicarbonate to protect your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the leucovorin? That helps reduce side effects, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. We start leucovorin about 24 hours after the methotrexate to 'rescue' your healthy cells. You’ll get it intravenously at first, then continue by mouth after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I remember from last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting your methotrexate infusion now. It will take a few hours. A nurse will monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I brought a book to pass the time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Infusion is complete. You tolerated it well. We’ll keep you on IV fluids and monitor your urine output and pH to make sure your kidneys stay protected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel fine so far. No nausea yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are stable. Urine pH has been above 7.5, which is where we want it. We’ll continue fluids and check your creatinine again later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I did feel a bit nauseous last night, but the medicine they gave me helped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common. We’ll keep ondansetron available for you as needed. Nausea usually resolves within a day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is there anything I should avoid eating or drinking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stick to the regular diet, but avoid citrus, carbonated drinks, vitamin C supplements, and fruits for now. They can interfere with methotrexate clearance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll skip the orange juice, then. What about my aspirin? I usually take it daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held it during the infusion to reduce bleeding risk, but you’ll restart it when you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had a bowel movement since I got here. Is that a concern?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not uncommon, especially with reduced activity and some medications. We’ll start you on lactulose to help, and continue your usual docusate and senna.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I’d like to avoid getting really backed up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your methotrexate level is coming down nicely. It’s now at 0.22, which means we’re close to discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Does that mean I can go home tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely. We’ll give you your last dose of IV leucovorin today, then send you home with oral leucovorin to take four times a day for three more days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Four tablets every six hours? That’s a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is, but it’s important to finish the full course to protect your bone marrow and gut lining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll set alarms so I don’t miss any.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The radiology report from your brain MRI came back. There’s no change from your last scan—no new tumors or signs of recurrence.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Is the spot in my frontal lobe still there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but it’s slightly smaller. It still looks like gliosis—scar tissue from the prior biopsy—nothing active.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no new treatment needed for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. We’ll keep monitoring it, but right now, the methotrexate is doing its job preventing lymphoma recurrence in the brain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried it might be growing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had a bowel movement? Great. We’ll keep you on docusate and senna as needed to prevent this from happening again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, finally. The lactulose worked. Should I keep taking it at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Only if needed. We’re sending you home with docusate twice daily and senna as needed. Increase fluids and fiber if you can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your methotrexate level is low enough, and you’re otherwise stable. We’re clearing you for discharge today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take the leucovorin four tablets every six hours for three full days. Continue docusate twice daily, senna if constipated, and restart your aspirin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I start feeling nauseous again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use the ondansetron—one tablet every eight hours as needed. But if vomiting becomes severe or you can’t keep fluids down, call us or come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the floaters? Should I expect them to improve?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They should start to fade over the next few weeks, as they have before. That’s a good sign the treatment is working in the eyes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my next chemo cycle?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That will be scheduled for next month. Your oncology team will contact you with the date.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, Doctor. I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You did well this admission. Go home, rest, and take your meds as directed. We’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just to confirm, the MRI showed no abnormal enhancement or new lesions. The small frontal focus is stable and likely gliosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you mentioned that yesterday. I’m glad it’s not getting worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And your PET scan from earlier shows the lymph nodes in your chest are no longer active. That’s a very good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the lymphoma is still in remission?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, both systemically and in the central nervous system. That’s why we continue these maintenance doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I’ll keep coming for these treatments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge paperwork is ready. Nurse will go over your medications one more time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I think I’ve got it all straight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If anything changes—like fever, severe nausea, or new neurological symptoms—don’t hesitate to call or come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Thompson. We’ll see you for your next cycle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I avoid crowds or sick people?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. Your immune system can be a bit suppressed after methotrexate, so yes, avoid close contact with anyone who’s sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll stay home as much as I can then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s wise. And keep washing your hands. Otherwise, you can resume normal activities as you feel up to it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m all packed and ready to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re discharged. Take it easy, follow your meds, and we’ll see you next month.
